query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build substrate during LPBF processing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder will reduce thermal gradients during solidification, thereby lowering residual stress, minimizing segregation and defect formation, and ultimately improving the mechanical integrity of the alloy relative to conventional processing.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with homogeneous composition but susceptible to rapid cooling-induced segregation, residual stresses, and defect formation during processing.
generation.intervention: Introduce an in-situ preheating step to elevate the build substrate and surrounding powder bed temperature (e.g., to 300–500 °C) during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) processing.
generation.conditions: This intervention is applied during LPBF processing under an inert atmosphere, using standard laser parameters aside from the preheat; post-fabrication mechanical testing is conducted at room temperature under quasi-static loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients during solidification which lead to finer, more uniform grain structures and mitigated phase segregation.
generation.mechanism: Elevated preheat temperatures lower the temperature differential between the molten pool and the surrounding material. This moderation of the cooling rate reduces the driving force for rapid solidification phenomena such as elemental segregation and defect (e.g., porosity, cracks) formation. In turn, this fosters a more homogeneous microstructure with lower residual stresses and enhanced mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The preheated LPBF process is expected to yield AlCrFeNiSi components with a more uniform microstructure, lower residual stress levels, reduced segregation at grain boundaries, and fewer processing-induced defects, resulting in improved yield strength and ductility compared to components fabricated under conventional (non-preheated) conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventional LPBF processing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powders at room temperature, which typically exhibits steep thermal gradients leading to higher residual stresses, pronounced segregation, and increased density of processing defects.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is valid for LPBF processing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi under controlled, inert atmospheres with standard laser parameters aside from the preheat intervention; extrapolation to other additive manufacturing methods or significantly different alloy compositions would require additional validation.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal preheat temperature range and the precise quantitative improvements in mechanical properties (e.g., percentage reduction in residual stresses or segregation) remain to be empirically determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform LPBF fabrication of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi samples under two conditions: one with in-situ preheating of the build substrate (set within the 300–500 °C range) and one without preheating (standard room temperature). Maintain identical laser and processing parameters for both groups. Following fabrication, use scanning electron microscopy and electron backscatter diffraction to evaluate microstructural uniformity and segregation, X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction to measure residual stresses, and conduct standardized mechanical tests (e.g., tensile and compressive tests) to assess strength and ductility.
measurements: Grain size distribution and segregation patterns
Mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, tensile/compressive strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the preheated LPBF samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in residual stresses, segregation, and defect density, or if their mechanical properties (strength and ductility) are not demonstrably improved compared to those fabricated without preheating.

Question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?. System: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at.% W, 20 at.% Ta, 20 at.% Mo, 20 at.% Nb, 20 at.% V). Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system (400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere); mixed elemental powders (20–70 µm) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; advanced trials parameters: 244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 0.10 mm hatch spacing, 0.03 mm layer thickness, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density, 67° layer rotation.. Test conditions: Density and Vickers hardness (HV10) measured; compression strength tested at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; electrochemical behavior assessed via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (scanning rate 0.5 mV/s)..
